Text | Fanyu Meng

Editing | Er Mu, Fanyu Meng

“... so I really have to make sure that the sound speaks of BMW’s identity. When you listen to it, it’s the sound of our history – and our future.”

The electric-car market was still fairly quiet last year. Then Apple suddenly announced it would build a car, the market took off, and in China Xiaomi and Didi have joined the rush too. There is no denying it: electric cars are the future of the automobile. China has been encouraging the production and use of electric vehicles for years, and other countries are no different. In the Netherlands, for example, more than 90% of the Teslas you see on the streets are company cars bought with government subsidies. Besides the well-known benefits of saving energy and protecting the environment, the biggest acoustic difference between an electric car and a combustion car is that the electric one is quieter. That is a good thing, but it doesn’t mean noise problems vanish and NVH engineers can be sent home. Sounds that the combustion engine used to mask, such as tire noise, become much more noticeable in an electric car. And electric cars produce prominent high-frequency noise, which, even at the same sound pressure level, is more unpleasant than the low-frequency-dominated sound of a combustion engine.

Beyond that, artificial sound is where much of the attention on electric cars goes. First, electric cars are so quiet that pedestrians can’t hear them coming, which makes accidents more likely. So both the United States and China have introduced minimum sound level requirements for electric vehicles, and the Acoustic Vehicle Alerting System (AVAS) was born. To put it simply: strap a big loudspeaker to an electric Ferrari and have it blare a discount-store jingle, “Everything two yuan! Everything two yuan!”, and not even noise-cancelling headphones may be able to block it. Pedestrians will hear it all right, and jump out of their skins. Second, since sound has to be added anyway, creative OEMs have let loose, treating the electric car as a musical instrument and designing distinctive sounds to build their brands. As the quote at the top says, a car needs to show its identity: in the sound it makes, you should hear the past, the present and the future. The goal is that, with your eyes closed, you can tell which brand of car just drove past.

One of my earlier articles includes a video of Mercedes-Benz’s AVAS, if you’re curious:

A history of acoustics: auralization

Renzo Vitale (the man on the cover), a colleague from my PhD days, now designs sound for electric cars at BMW headquarters in Germany. He is also a pianist and an artist, and these days he is BMW’s main face for the media, appearing on all sorts of programs; not long ago he even gave a TED talk. He looks for inspiration at the piano, or improvises a piece of music, and then tries it out in the car. I don’t know how far he has got, but that is his everyday job, and it sounds very exciting. Actually doing it is less rosy than it sounds, though. The sound you design has to match what the car is really doing. When the car accelerates, for example, you need to hear the frequency rise smoothly and continuously, and the changes in level and frequency have to follow certain rules. Our ears and our experience are extremely picky: when a sound doesn’t match what we expect, it backfires. It just feels strange, and you would have been better off with no sound design at all.

Here is an example. When we synthesize combustion-engine noise, we can use the empirical formulas below to generate the engine sound of a moving car [1]. The vehicle speed v(t) is linearly related to the engine speed n(t). A signal is synthesized for each engine order m, and the signals are summed. The order sound pressure levels can be looked up in tables. Of course this is only a very rough estimate of the signal; reality is far more complicated. And if you also want to slip in a sonic brand identity, there is a great deal more to consider.

A quick preview: a few years ago Like Jiang, one of the authors of this WeChat account, and I published two papers on using acoustic virtual reality to assess urban sound environments. In a while (a few months?) I’ll turn them into n (1–2?) popular-science articles, so stay tuned. The formulas below are the ones I used to synthesize sound back then.

Back to the topic. When it comes to sound synthesis, the sound artists at the big carmakers will try anything. The Audi designer below, for example, voices an electric car with a power drill and an electric guitar. Layer a few tracks together and, believe it or not, it sounds just right.

Watch the video · Want your own million-yuan electric supercar? All it takes is a guitar ➕ a power drill~ With Apple, Xiaomi and Didi joining, the electric-car industry…

As living standards rise and our idea of the car changes, the car of the future will no longer be just a way of getting around. It will gradually become an electronic product, like a phone or a computer. Conversations about cars will no longer be only about speed, safety and fuel consumption; words like interior, software and comfort will come up more and more. For this we can thank Elon Musk’s imagination, which has opened up endless possibilities for the car industry, supposedly a “sunset industry.” We should also thank Tesla’s factory in China, which not only kept him from going bankrupt but made him, briefly and gloriously, the richest man in the world.

Acoustics lives on the upper floors of Maslow’s hierarchy of needs, and it is bound to play an ever larger role as cars develop. In electroacoustics, acoustics is jokingly called black magic, and as far as I can see, automotive sound design is no different. The keys will be regulating the market, establishing international standards and finding the right methods for sound design. At the same time, with the roar of the combustion engine gone, there is boundless room for imagination: to design sounds, to tap the wealth of information that sound can carry, and to make it carry the value of a brand.

References

[1] Pieren, R. D. (2018). Auralization of Environmental Acoustical Sceneries: Synthesis of Road Traffic, Railway and Wind Turbine Noise (Doctoral dissertation, Delft University of Technology).

[2] Automotive testing technology international, November 2020
